opus-5.5.text:
I think what I admire most about Yann is his conviction. He's someone who has held onto a set of beliefs for decades, sometimes when almost nobody else in the field shared them. Back in the period when neural networks were deeply unfashionable, he kept working on convolutional networks because he believed it was the right direction. History proved him right, but at the time that took real courage and patience.

Even today, when he's already won the Turing Award and could easily ride the mainstream wave, he's still willing to be contrarian. He openly says large language models alone won't get us to human-level intelligence, and that we need world models, systems that learn from observing the physical world the way babies and animals do. You can agree or disagree with him, but he says it clearly, he argues for it, and he puts his research where his mouth is. I find that very rare and very refreshing.

The second thing is his commitment to openness. He's been a strong advocate for open research and open-source models, and he really believes that science advances faster when knowledge is shared rather than locked up inside a few companies. For a researcher, that resonates a lot with me.

On a personal level, he's also just very genuine. He's curious about everything: he builds things, he plays music, he loves sailing and building model airplanes. He still gets excited about ideas like a student. Being around him reminds you why you got into research in the first place: not for the hype, but because these are some of the most fascinating questions there are.

fable-5.1.text:
What I admire most about Yann is that he has stayed completely himself for forty years. He has had the same core belief since the 1980s, that machines should learn representations from data, and he kept pushing it through the long winter when almost nobody in the field wanted to hear it. Convolutional networks were not fashionable when he built them. He didn't care. He just kept going.

And when the field finally came around and he had every reason to sit back and enjoy it, he did the opposite. He started telling everyone that what we have now is not enough, that autoregressive language models are not the path to real intelligence, that we need world models, self-supervised learning, systems that understand the physical world. He takes positions that are deeply unpopular, and he takes them in public, with his name on them, knowing he will get attacked for it. That takes a particular kind of courage that is rare in science, and even rarer once you have a Turing Award and could just coast.

The second thing is how he treats younger people. When I was at FAIR, Yann would argue with a first-year PhD student exactly the same way he would argue with a senior professor. He didn't pull rank. If you had a good argument he listened, and if you had a bad one he told you, but he was never dismissive. He genuinely believes ideas should win on their own merit, and he lives that. That environment shaped how I think about research.

And honestly, he is still curious. He still reads papers, he still wants to understand what a new result actually means rather than just whether it got a good number. A lot of people lose that. He hasn't. That, to me, is what a scientist is supposed to look like.

astra-6.text:
What I admire about Yann is his intellectual independence. He’s willing to pursue an idea even when it isn’t fashionable, and to argue for it openly. In research, it’s easy to let the prevailing consensus determine which questions you work on. I admire the willingness to step back and ask whether that consensus is actually right.

That doesn’t mean you have to agree with every position he takes. It’s the combination of conviction and willingness to engage in debate that I find valuable. You want people in the field who push you to examine your assumptions.
